name: Space & the Planets (AI-written, not yet reviewed)
description: 71 questions on space, the planets and space exploration, from easy to hard (19 easy, 24 medium, 28 hard), written by Claude. Every question and answer needs checking by a person before anybody plays it.

source.name: Written by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) on 2026-10-05, from its own knowledge plus the pages each item cites: no API call. Each item's `source` names the page its fact was confirmed on, or "common knowledge" with a reason where the fact is universal. Fact-check pending: no item carries `checked` yet, so a separate fact-check pass still has to go through every item, and a person still reviews it by playing.

review.how: Check every question, answer and explanation. Fix or delete what is wrong, set status to 'reviewed' with your name and the date, then move the file to packs/ and list it in pack_library.js.

items.question: Which star is closest to Earth?
items.explain: Our own Sun is a star, and it is by far the nearest one to us.

source.note: Universally taught that the Sun is the nearest star.

items.question: Which planet is famous for its beautiful wide rings?
items.explain: Saturn's rings are made of billions of chunks of ice and rock.

items.question: In what year did astronauts first land on the Moon?
items.explain: Apollo 11 landed on the Moon in July 1969.

items.question: Which planet is closest to the Sun?
items.explain: Little Mercury is the innermost planet, closest to the Sun.

source.note: Basic order of the planets, taught universally.

items.question: About how long does Earth take to travel once around the Sun?
items.explain: One trip around the Sun takes about 365 days - that is our year.

items.question: What is Pluto called today?
items.explain: In 2006 astronomers reclassified Pluto as a dwarf planet.

items.question: The Big Dipper points the way to which famous star?
items.explain: The two stars at the end of the Dipper's cup point to Polaris, the North Star.

items.question: Which country launched Sputnik, the first satellite, in 1957?
items.explain: The Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1 on October 4, 1957, starting the Space Age.

items.question: Who was the first American woman in space?
items.explain: Sally Ride flew on the space shuttle Challenger in June 1983.

items.question: Who was the first person to travel into space?
items.explain: Yuri Gagarin orbited Earth on April 12, 1961.

items.question: Which constellation has three bright stars in a row called its belt?
items.explain: Orion the Hunter wears a belt of three bright stars in a nearly straight line.

items.question: Which planet has a giant storm called the Great Red Spot?
items.explain: Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a storm wider than Earth.

items.question: What is the Sun?
items.explain: The Sun is a star - a huge, hot, glowing ball of gas.

items.question: How many planets are in our solar system?
items.explain: There are eight planets, from Mercury out to Neptune.

source.note: Eight planets under the IAU definition since 2006; universally taught.

items.question: Counting out from the Sun, which planet is Earth?
items.explain: Earth is the third planet from the Sun, after Mercury and Venus.

items.question: What does ISS stand for?
items.explain: People first moved aboard the International Space Station in November 2000.

items.question: Which famous space telescope was carried into orbit by a space shuttle in 1990?
items.explain: The shuttle Discovery launched the Hubble Space Telescope in 1990.

items.question: Which astronaut walked on the Moon alongside Neil Armstrong?
items.explain: Buzz Aldrin flew the lunar module Eagle down with Armstrong in 1969.

items.question: What is a shooting star, really?
answers: A meteor burning up in our sky
items.correct: A meteor burning up in our sky
items.explain: A shooting star is a bit of space rock or dust burning up as it hits our air.

source.note: Basic, widely known explanation of meteors.

items.question: Which planet is the hottest in our solar system?
items.explain: Venus's thick clouds trap heat, making it even hotter than Mercury.

items.question: What was the name of the Apollo 11 lunar module that landed on the Moon?
items.explain: The Eagle landed, while the command module Columbia waited in orbit.

items.question: Where on the Moon did Apollo 11 land?
items.explain: Eagle touched down in the Sea of Tranquility on July 20, 1969.

items.question: Which Apollo 11 astronaut piloted the command module while the other two landed?
items.explain: Michael Collins flew the command module Columbia around the Moon.

items.question: About how long does sunlight take to reach Earth?
items.explain: Sunlight crosses about 93 million miles to us in roughly 8 minutes.

items.question: What did John Glenn name the spacecraft he orbited Earth in, in 1962?
items.explain: Glenn circled Earth three times in Friendship 7 on February 20, 1962.

items.question: Who was the first woman to fly in space?
items.explain: Soviet cosmonaut Valentina Tereshkova flew in June 1963.

items.question: What are the names of the two moons of Mars?
items.explain: They are named for the horses that pulled the chariot of Ares, the Greek god of war.

items.question: What is the name of the giant Martian volcano, the largest in the solar system?
items.explain: Olympus Mons is over 25 miles tall, with a base the size of Arizona.

items.question: Which planet is less dense than water, so it could float in a giant bathtub?
items.explain: Saturn is the only planet less dense than water.

items.question: Who discovered the planet Uranus in 1781?
items.explain: Herschel at first thought he had found a comet or a star.

items.question: On Venus, the Sun rises in which direction?
items.explain: Venus spins backward compared with most planets, so the Sun rises in the west.

items.question: What is the largest moon of Saturn?
items.explain: Hazy Titan even has lakes of liquid methane on its surface.

items.question: What is the largest moon in the whole solar system?
items.explain: Jupiter's moon Ganymede is even bigger than the planet Mercury.

items.question: Who discovered Jupiter's four largest moons in 1610?
items.explain: Galileo spotted Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto with an early telescope.

items.question: Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky, has what nickname?
items.explain: Sirius is the brightest star in Canis Major, the Big Dog.

items.question: On Christmas Eve 1968, the Apollo 8 crew became the first people to do what?
items.explain: Circling the Moon, Bill Anders took the famous Earthrise photo.

items.question: Which space shuttle made the very first shuttle flight, in April 1981?
items.explain: John Young and Robert Crippen flew Columbia on the first shuttle mission.

items.question: The James Webb Space Telescope launched on which holiday in 2021?
items.explain: Webb lifted off on December 25, 2021, aboard an Ariane 5 rocket.

items.question: Who led the committee that chose what went on the Voyager Golden Record?
items.explain: Carl Sagan of Cornell led the group that picked the record's sounds and images.

items.question: Who became the first African American woman in space, in 1992?
items.explain: Mae Jemison, a doctor and engineer, flew on the shuttle Endeavour.

items.question: The word "cereal" shares its name with which dwarf planet?
items.explain: Both are named for Ceres, the Roman goddess of harvests and grain.

items.question: About how often does Halley's Comet come back around?
items.explain: Halley last came by in 1986 and is due back in 2061.

items.question: The Perseid meteor shower peaks in which month?
items.explain: The Perseids light up summer skies every mid-August.

items.question: Which planet was the first found by mathematical prediction rather than by spotting it in the sky?
items.explain: Urbain Le Verrier calculated where Neptune should be, and it was found there in 1846.

items.question: Which astronomer confirmed Neptune through a telescope at the Berlin Observatory in 1846?
items.explain: Galle found Neptune right where Le Verrier's math said it would be.

items.question: The moons of Uranus are named for characters created by which two writers?
items.explain: Moons like Miranda and Ariel come from William Shakespeare and Alexander Pope.

items.question: William Herschel tried to name Uranus after whom?
items.explain: The royal name did not stick; Johann Bode's suggestion, Uranus, won out.

items.question: Who first suggested the name "Pluto" in 1930?
items.explain: Venetia Burney, an 11-year-old in Oxford, England, proposed it over breakfast.

items.question: On what date did NASA's New Horizons fly past Pluto?
items.explain: New Horizons made the only close visit to Pluto on July 14, 2015.

items.question: Which space shuttle flew the first Hubble servicing mission in 1993 to fix its flawed optics?
items.explain: Endeavour's crew corrected Hubble's vision in 1993.

items.question: Where is the James Webb Space Telescope stationed?
answers: In low Earth orbit like Hubble
At the second Lagrange point, about a million miles from Earth
items.correct: At the second Lagrange point, about a million miles from Earth
items.explain: Webb orbits the Sun at L2, about 1 million miles from Earth.

items.question: Why are the James Webb Space Telescope's mirrors coated with gold?
answers: Gold reflects infrared light very well
items.correct: Gold reflects infrared light very well
items.explain: Webb sees in infrared, and gold reflects those wavelengths efficiently.

items.question: In what year did Voyager 1 cross into interstellar space?
items.explain: Voyager 1 crossed in 2012; its twin Voyager 2 followed in 2018.

items.question: Explorer 1, America's first satellite, discovered what around Earth?
items.explain: James Van Allen's instrument on Explorer 1 revealed belts of radiation in 1958.

items.question: On which 1966 mission did Neil Armstrong make the first docking of two vehicles in orbit?
items.explain: Armstrong and David Scott docked with a target vehicle on Gemini 8 in March 1966.

items.question: Neil Armstrong's first NACA job, in 1955, was at a laboratory in which city?
items.explain: He started at the Lewis Flight Propulsion Laboratory in Cleveland, Ohio.

items.question: Before it was renamed for John Glenn in 1999, NASA's Cleveland research center was named after whom?
items.explain: It was the Lewis Research Center, honoring NACA research director George W. Lewis.

items.question: Apollo 17, the last crewed Moon landing, touched down in which lunar valley?
items.explain: Gene Cernan and geologist Harrison Schmitt explored Taurus-Littrow in December 1972.

items.question: In 2005, the Huygens probe made the first landing in the outer solar system. Where did it land?
items.explain: ESA's Huygens parachuted onto Saturn's moon Titan on January 14, 2005.

items.question: Galileo announced Jupiter's moons in a 1610 book with what title?
answers: Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems
On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres
items.explain: Sidereus Nuncius, or The Starry Messenger, came out in March 1610.

items.question: At which observatory did Edwin Hubble show in 1923 that Andromeda is a separate galaxy?
items.explain: Hubble used the 100-inch Hooker Telescope at Mount Wilson in California.

items.question: About 14,000 years ago, Earth's north pole pointed toward which bright star instead of Polaris?
items.explain: Earth's slow wobble moves the pole; it will point near Vega again in about 12,000 years.

items.question: The Mars spot where Ingenuity made the first powered flight on another planet was named what?
items.explain: It honors the Wright brothers of Dayton, Ohio; Ingenuity first flew on April 19, 2021.

items.question: Which comet leaves behind the dust that makes the Perseid meteor shower?
items.explain: Comet Swift-Tuttle takes 133 years to orbit the Sun.

items.question: Which October meteor shower comes from debris left by Halley's Comet?
items.explain: Halley feeds both the Orionids in October and the Eta Aquarids in May.

items.question: Who discovered Ceres in 1801, the first object found in the asteroid belt?
items.explain: Piazzi's find, Ceres, is now counted as a dwarf planet.

items.question: How long does Venus take to spin once on its axis?
items.explain: Venus's 243-day spin is longer than its 225-day year.

items.question: Which of Neptune's moons orbits backward, suggesting it was captured?
items.explain: Triton's retrograde orbit hints it was once a separate world Neptune captured.

items.question: Which spacecraft carried Valentina Tereshkova on her 1963 flight?
items.explain: Vostok 6 circled Earth 48 times in about 71 hours.

items.question: The first space shuttle launch, on April 12, 1981, came exactly 20 years after what?
items.explain: Gagarin flew on April 12, 1961; Columbia launched on the same date in 1981.

items.question: From which launch site did Sputnik 1 lift off in 1957?
items.explain: Sputnik launched from what is now the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan.
